questions.question: Which of the following substances would make the best primary standard?
questions.answer: A primary standard must be of high purity, soluble enough to make a standard solution, and have a high formula (molar) mass so that the mass weighed is large and the percentage weighing error is small. Only Q has all three properties (B).
options: Substance P: purity high, solubility low, formula mass low
Substance Q: purity high, solubility high, formula mass high
Substance R: purity high, solubility low, formula mass high
Substance S: purity high, solubility high, formula mass low

questions.question: "An acid is a substance that donates one or more protons." Who first gave this definition of an acid?
questions.answer: Defining an acid as a proton ($\text{H}^+$) donor is the Brønsted–Lowry definition (B). Arrhenius defined acids as producing $\text{H}^+$ in water, Lewis as electron-pair acceptors, and Lavoisier as substances containing oxygen.

questions.question: The table shows the pH range of four acid–base indicators: W 3.3–4.3; X 6.2–7.5; Y 7.8–10.3; Z 8.1–9.8. Which indicator would be the best choice for a titration between potassium hydroxide and ethanoic acid?
questions.answer: KOH is a strong base and ethanoic acid a weak acid. At the equivalence point the solution contains the ethanoate ion, a weak base, so the pH is above 7 (about 8.5–9). The indicator must change colour in this region: Y and Z both do, but Z (8.1–9.8) has the narrower range centred on the equivalence point, giving a sharper end-point (D).

questions.question: What is the correct systematic name for the following compound? (A butane chain, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(R)CH(R)CH}_3$, with an ethyl group on each of the two middle carbons.)
questions.answer: The longest carbon chain is 6 carbons (one ethyl group forms part of the main chain), so the parent is hexane with a methyl group on each of carbons 3 and 4: 3,4-dimethylhexane (C).

questions.question: The structure of a compound is shown. It has been suggested that this molecule may be an effective drug for treating influenza. Which row of the table correctly names the functional groups labelled I, II and III?
questions.answer: Group I is –COOH (carboxylic acid); group II is –$\text{NH}_2$ attached to an alkyl carbon (amine); group III is –NH–C(=O)–$\text{CH}_3$ (amide) (B).
options: I: aldehyde; II: amide; III: ester
I: carboxylic acid; II: amine; III: amide
I: ketone; II: amine; III: carboxylic acid
I: carboxylic acid; II: amide; III: amine

questions.question: Which of the following diagrams represents a micelle that forms in water when soap is used to remove grease from dirty dishes?
questions.answer: A soap molecule has a charged hydrophilic head and a non-polar hydrocarbon tail. In water the tails point inwards, dissolving the non-polar grease in the centre, and the charged heads point outwards towards the water, so the micelle can be carried away (B).

questions.question: How many structural isomers are there for the compound with molecular formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{BrCl}$?
questions.answer: The compound is a propane chain with one Br and one Cl on different (or the same) carbons. The isomers are: 1-bromo-1-chloropropane, 2-bromo-2-chloropropane, 1-bromo-2-chloropropane, 2-bromo-1-chloropropane and 1-bromo-3-chloropropane: 5 (B).

questions.question: Which titration curve best represents the change in pH as $0.100$ M NaOH solution is added to a $10.0$ mL aliquot of $0.100$ M HCl solution?
questions.answer: The pH starts low (about 1) and rises as NaOH is added. At the equivalence point, $10.0$ mL ($0.010$ L) of NaOH, there is a sharp rise through pH 7, and after that the pH levels out at a high value (about 12–13 for excess strong base) (D). A and C fall (acid added to base), and B levels out too low (pH about 10).

questions.question: A $0.10$ M solution of fluoride ions is gradually added to a solution containing $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ ions, each at $1\times10^{-3}$ M. In what order, from first to last, will the precipitates of $\text{BaF}_2$, $\text{CaF}_2$ and $\text{PbF}_2$ form? ($K_{sp}$: $\text{BaF}_2$ $1.8\times10^{-7}$; $\text{CaF}_2$ $1.5\times10^{-10}$; $\text{PbF}_2$ $7.1\times10^{-7}$)
questions.answer: A precipitate forms when $[\text{F}^-]^2[\text{M}^{2+}]>K_{sp}$, so $[\text{F}^-]=\sqrt{K_{sp}/10^{-3}}$ is needed: $\text{CaF}_2$: $3.9\times10^{-4}$ M; $\text{BaF}_2$: $1.3\times10^{-2}$ M; $\text{PbF}_2$: $2.7\times10^{-2}$ M. The lowest fluoride concentration is needed first, so the order is $\text{CaF}_2$, $\text{BaF}_2$, $\text{PbF}_2$ (D).

questions.question: Methanoic acid ($K_a=1.82\times10^{-4}$) and ethanoic acid ($K_a=1.74\times10^{-5}$) are both weak acids at $25^\circ$C. Two separate solutions were prepared, one of $0.1$ M methanoic acid and the other of $0.1$ M ethanoic acid. Which one of the following would be present in the lowest concentration at $25^\circ$C?
questions.answer: Both acids are mostly un-ionised (about 0.1 M). The ethanoic acid is the weaker acid, so it ionises less: $[\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-]=\sqrt{1.74\times10^{-5}\times0.1}=1.3\times10^{-3}$ M, compared with $[\text{HCOO}^-]=\sqrt{1.82\times10^{-4}\times0.1}=4.3\times10^{-3}$ M. The lowest concentration is $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ (B).
options: HCOOH in the methanoic acid solution

questions.question: A solution contains an equilibrium mixture of two cobalt(II) ions: $\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6^{2+}(aq)+4\text{Cl}^-(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}(aq)+6\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$ (pink / blue). The solution is purple. Which one of the following changes would cause 10 mL of the purple solution to turn blue?
questions.answer: To turn blue, the equilibrium must shift to the right. Adding concentrated HCl increases $[\text{Cl}^-]$ (and by Le Chatelier's principle the system shifts to use up $\text{Cl}^-$), forming more blue $\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}$ (A). Silver nitrate removes $\text{Cl}^-$ as AgCl (shift left, pink); water dilutes and shifts left; a catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium.
options: the addition of a few drops of 10 M hydrochloric acid at a constant temperature
the addition of a few drops of 0.1 M silver nitrate at a constant temperature
the addition of a few drops of a catalyst at a constant temperature
the addition of a few drops of water at a constant temperature

questions.question: One litre of an aqueous solution of potassium hydroxide (KOH) has a pH of 12.0 at $25^\circ$C. How many moles of pure HCl gas must be added to the solution to lower the pH from pH 12.0 to 2.0?
questions.answer: $0.01$ mol of $\text{OH}^-$ (pH 12) must be neutralised by $0.01$ mol HCl, then a further $0.01$ mol HCl gives $[\text{H}^+]=10^{-2}$ M (pH 2): $0.02$ mol (C).

questions.question: Hydrogen iodide is produced by the reaction between hydrogen and iodine: $\text{H}_2(g)+\text{I}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{HI}(g)$. Experiment 1 was carried out at constant temperature. Experiment 2 was a repeat of experiment 1 at a different temperature. The graph shows the amount of HI produced over time for the two experiments. These results show that experiment 2 was conducted at a:
questions.answer: Experiment 2 reaches equilibrium sooner (its curve rises faster), so the rate is higher and it was at a higher temperature. Its equilibrium yield of HI is lower, so raising the temperature shifted the equilibrium to the left, which means the forward reaction is exothermic (D).
options: lower temperature than experiment 1 and the reaction is endothermic.
lower temperature than experiment 1 and the reaction is exothermic.
higher temperature than experiment 1 and the reaction is endothermic.
higher temperature than experiment 1 and the reaction is exothermic.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements about $10.0$ mL of $0.10$ M HCl and $10.0$ mL of $0.10$ M $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ solutions is true?
questions.answer: Both acids are monoprotic with the same number of moles ($1.0\times10^{-3}$ mol), so each neutralises exactly $1.0\times10^{-3}$ mol NaOH (A). The weak acid ionises only slightly, so it has fewer ions (lower conductivity), a lower $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ and reacts more slowly with magnesium than HCl.
options: Each solution will react completely with $10.0$ mL of $0.10$ M NaOH solution.
Each solution will have the same electrical conductivity.
Each solution will react at the same rate with 1.00 g of magnesium ribbon.
The concentration of $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ ions will be greater in the $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ solution.

questions.question: Halothane (1-bromo-1-chloro-2,2,2-trifluoroethane) is a general anaesthetic. The diagram represents the reaction pathway that produces it: molecule X ($\text{Cl}_2\text{C=CHCl}$) →(HF, $\text{SbCl}_3$, 130 °C, step 1)→ $\text{CF}_3\text{CHCl}_2$ →($\text{Br}_2$, 450 °C, step 2)→ $\text{CF}_3\text{CHBrCl}$. Which of the following correctly identifies molecule X and the type of reaction shown in step 2?
questions.answer: Molecule X has a carbon–carbon double bond with three chlorine atoms: 1,1,2-trichloroethene. In step 2 a hydrogen atom is replaced by a bromine atom (with $\text{Br}_2$ at high temperature), with no double bond involved, so it is a substitution reaction (C).

questions.question: Four different equilibrium systems (I–IV) at standard pressure and temperature are shown: I $\text{N}_2(g)+3\text{H}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{NH}_3(g)$, $\Delta H<0$; II $2\text{NOBr}(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{NO}(g)+\text{Br}_2(g)$, $\Delta H<0$; III $\text{N}_2(g)+2\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{NO}_2(g)$, $\Delta H>0$; IV $\text{PCl}_5(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{PCl}_3(g)+\text{Cl}_2(g)$, $\Delta H>0$. In each system, the pressure was increased. Later, the temperature was decreased. In which equilibrium system would BOTH changes result in a product yield increase?
questions.answer: Increasing the pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas: I (4→2) and III (3→2) increase their yield; II and IV do not (they produce more moles). Decreasing the temperature favours the exothermic direction: I ($\Delta H<0$) increases its yield, but III ($\Delta H>0$) does not. Only system I satisfies both (A).

questions.question: A student heated $250$ mL of water by burning methanol in a spirit burner. The enthalpy of combustion of methanol is $-726\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Assume that all heat released is absorbed by the water. What is the maximum change in temperature of the water when $1.26$ g of methanol is completely combusted?

A particular reaction can occur with or without a catalyst. The energy profiles of this reaction, both catalysed and uncatalysed, are shown. Which row of the table best matches the reactions as shown by the energy profiles? (Columns: $E_a$ uncatalysed, $\Delta H$ uncatalysed, $E_a$ catalysed, $\Delta H$ catalysed, all in kJ mol$^{-1}$.)
questions.answer: The uncatalysed profile peaks at $+80$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ above the reactants, so $E_a=80$; the products end $70$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ below the reactants, $\Delta H=-70$. The catalysed profile (dashed) peaks at $60$, so $E_a=60$, but the same reactants and products give the same $\Delta H=-70$. Activation energies are never negative (C).

questions.question: Consider the reaction $\text{SO}_2(g)+\text{NO}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{SO}_3(g)+\text{NO}(g)$, with $K_{eq}=33$. If $0.10$ mol each of $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{NO}_2$ are placed in a $1.0$ L container, what is the concentration of $\text{SO}_3$ at equilibrium?
questions.answer: Let $x=[\text{SO}_3]=[\text{NO}]$ at equilibrium, with $[\text{SO}_2]=[\text{NO}_2]=0.10-x$: $K_{eq}=\dfrac{x^2}{(0.10-x)^2}=33\Rightarrow\dfrac{x}{0.10-x}=\sqrt{33}=5.74\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{0.574}{6.74}=0.085$ M (C).

questions.question: An experiment is conducted in which 4-aminobutanoic acid, $\text{H}_2\text{N(CH}_2)_3\text{COOH}$, forms a polymer containing 100 monomer units. What is the molar mass of this polymer?
questions.answer: This is a condensation polymerisation, releasing one water molecule for each bond formed. $M$(monomer) $=103.12$ g mol$^{-1}$. For 100 units there are 99 amide links (99 water molecules lost): $M=100(103.12)-99(18.02)=1.031\times10^4-1.784\times10^3=8.5\times10^3$ g mol$^{-1}$ (A).

questions.question: Carbon monoxide and hydrogen can be produced from methane and steam: $\text{CH}_4(g)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{CO}(g)+3\text{H}_2(g)$, $\Delta H=+206\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Some methane and steam were placed in a closed container and allowed to react at a fixed temperature. The graph shows the changes in concentration of methane and carbon monoxide as the reaction progresses. On the graph, draw a line to predict the change in concentration of hydrogen gas as the reaction progresses. Label this line '$\text{H}_2$'.
questions.answer: The $\text{H}_2$ starts at zero concentration and increases (it is a product), reaching a constant value when equilibrium is established at the same time as the other curves level off. Since $3$ mol of $\text{H}_2$ form for each mole of CO, the equilibrium concentration of $\text{H}_2$ is three times that of CO (the curve rises to three times the height of the CO line, and three times as steeply initially) (see graph).

questions.question: On the graph, draw a line to show how the formation of carbon monoxide would differ over time in the presence of a catalyst.
questions.answer: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner but the equilibrium position is unchanged. The CO curve should rise more steeply from the origin and level off earlier, at the same final concentration as the original curve (see graph).

questions.question: A student conducted an experiment in the school laboratory to synthesise an ester. Some of the equipment used is shown in the diagram (a vertical condenser 'X' on a flask heated by a Bunsen burner). Identify the risk associated with the student's experimental set-up in the diagram and suggest alternative equipment.
questions.answer: **Risk:** the flask is heated with a Bunsen burner (open flame) and the reaction mixture contains flammable, volatile organic liquids (alcohol and ester), so there is a fire risk. **Alternative:** heat with a hotplate, heating mantle or hot water bath instead of an open flame.

questions.question: Outline how the equipment piece labelled 'X' assisted in maximising the yield of the ester.
questions.answer: The water-cooled condenser condenses vaporised reactants and products so that they return to the reaction flask as liquid, preventing the loss of volatile substances to the atmosphere and so maximising the yield.

questions.question: Identify what else the student could do to maximise the yield of ester.
questions.answer: Add a small amount of concentrated sulfuric acid, which acts as a dehydrating agent and removes water, driving the equilibrium towards the ester (or: use an excess of one of the reactants to shift the equilibrium to the right; or heat the mixture for an extended time under reflux).

questions.question: Industrially, ethanol is made by fermentation of a sugar such as glucose with yeast in an aqueous solution. Write a balanced equation to show the production of $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ from $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$ and yeast.
questions.answer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6(aq)\xrightarrow{\text{yeast (zymase)}}2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}(aq)+2\text{CO}_2(g)$

questions.question: You carried out this fermentation reaction in the laboratory. What conditions were necessary for this fermentation to occur?
questions.answer: Any two of: the presence of yeast (enzymes as catalyst); absence of oxygen (anaerobic conditions); a temperature of about 37 °C (an optimum range of roughly 25–40 °C, not too hot, which would denature the enzymes); an aqueous solution of the sugar.

questions.question: Determine the mass, in grams, of pure $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ that would be produced from $1.25$ kg of $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$ dissolved in water.
questions.answer:
$n(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6)=\dfrac{1250}{180.16}=6.938$ mol. One mole of glucose gives 2 mol of ethanol: $n(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH})=13.88$ mol.
$$m=13.88\times46.07=639\ \text{g}$$
(Using $M=180$ and $46$ gives $613$ g; the marking guide accepted both.)

questions.question: Some salts display amphiprotic behaviour. Using a suitable example, explain what is meant by 'amphiprotic'. Support your answer using appropriate equations.
questions.answer:
A substance is amphiprotic if it can act as both a Brønsted–Lowry acid (proton donor) and a Brønsted–Lowry base (proton acceptor), depending on what it reacts with. Example: sodium hydrogencarbonate, whose $\text{HCO}_3^-$ ion:

- acts as an acid by donating a proton to a base: $\text{HCO}_3^-(aq)+\text{OH}^-(aq)\rightarrow\text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$
- acts as a base by accepting a proton from an acid: $\text{HCO}_3^-(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)\rightarrow\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$

questions.question: Scientists have developed biopolymers to replace traditional polymers. Polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB), made in the cells of microorganisms such as *Bacillus* using agricultural residue such as sugarcane bagasse as a carbon source, was developed as an alternative to polypropylene (PP), made from crude oil. Outline the advantage of using PHB as a replacement for PP.
questions.answer: PHB is made from renewable resources (plant waste) rather than finite fossil fuels (crude oil), and it is biodegradable (broken down by microorganisms) whereas polypropylene persists in the environment.

questions.question: What type of polymerisation reaction produces PHB and PP? (Monomers: hydroxybutyrate, $\text{HOCH(CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$; propylene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2$.)
questions.answer: **PHB: condensation polymerisation** (the –OH of one monomer reacts with the –COOH of another, forming an ester link and releasing water). **PP: addition polymerisation** (the C=C double bonds open and join with no loss of atoms).

questions.question: Draw three repeating units for each of the polymers made from the monomers (PHB from hydroxybutyrate and PP from propylene).
questions.answer:
**PHB** (three repeating units of the ester link):
$$\cdots-\text{O}-\text{CH(CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{C(=O)}-\text{O}-\text{CH(CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{C(=O)}-\text{O}-\text{CH(CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{C(=O)}-\cdots$$
**PP** (three repeating units; the polymer continues in both directions):
$$\cdots-\text{CH(CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\cdots$$
(see the structures drawn in the marking guide).

questions.question: Nitric oxide is formed during lightning strikes: $\text{N}_2(g)+\text{O}_2(g)\rightarrow2\text{NO}(g)$, $\Delta H=+180.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. The table shows $\Delta G$ at different temperatures: 2000 K: 131; 4000 K: 81; 6000 K: 31; 8000 K: −19; 10 000 K: −69 (kJ mol$^{-1}$). Graph the provided data (draw a labelled graph of $\Delta G$ against temperature).
questions.answer: Plot temperature (K) on the horizontal axis and $\Delta G$ (kJ mol$^{-1}$) on the vertical axis, using an appropriate scale, plot the five points (as crosses) and draw a line of best fit. The data fall on a straight line of gradient $-0.025\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ (see graph).

questions.question: Use the graph to estimate the minimum temperature in °C at which this reaction will become spontaneous. Justify your answer.
questions.answer: The line crosses $\Delta G=0$ at about $7200$ K (the line is $\Delta G=181-0.025T$, giving $7240$ K), so $T\approx7200-273\approx6900\ ^\circ\text{C}$ (the school's estimate was $6927^\circ$C). A reaction is spontaneous when $\Delta G<0$; above this temperature $\Delta G$ is negative, so the reaction becomes spontaneous at temperatures above about $6900\ ^\circ\text{C}$ (at exactly $\Delta G=0$ the system is at equilibrium).

questions.question: A mixture has $0.400$ mol each of $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2$ in a $2.00$ L vessel kept at $980^\circ$C. The reaction is $\text{CO}_2(g)+\text{H}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{CO}(g)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$, $\Delta H=+41.2\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. At this temperature the equilibrium concentration of CO is $0.110$ mol L$^{-1}$. Write the equilibrium constant expression for this reaction.
questions.answer: $$K_{eq}=\frac{[\text{CO}][\text{H}_2\text{O}]}{[\text{CO}_2][\text{H}_2]}$$ (all species are gases, so water is included).

questions.question: What is the equilibrium concentration of $\text{H}_2$ in the above equilibrium ($0.400$ mol each of $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2$ initially in a $2.00$ L vessel; $[\text{CO}]_{eq}=0.110$ mol L$^{-1}$)?
Calculate the equilibrium constant at 980 °C for the above equilibrium.
How would increasing the temperature affect the equilibrium constant for the above equilibrium ($\Delta H=+41.2\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$)? Explain your answer.
questions.answer: $K_{eq}$ would increase. The forward reaction is endothermic ($\Delta H>0$), so by Le Chatelier's principle a temperature increase shifts the equilibrium to the right to absorb heat. The concentrations of the products (CO and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$) increase and those of the reactants decrease, so the ratio $\dfrac{[\text{CO}][\text{H}_2\text{O}]}{[\text{CO}_2][\text{H}_2]}$ increases.

questions.question: Lead(II) carbonate is a sparingly soluble salt ($K_{sp}=7.40\times10^{-14}$ at $25^\circ$C). Calculate the molar solubility of lead(II) carbonate in water at $25^\circ$C. Show all working.
questions.answer:
$\text{PbCO}_3(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Pb}^{2+}(aq)+\text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq)$. Let the solubility be $s$: $K_{sp}=[\text{Pb}^{2+}][\text{CO}_3^{2-}]=s^2=7.40\times10^{-14}$
$$s=2.72\times10^{-7}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

questions.question: Quantitatively compare the solubility of lead(II) carbonate in water with its solubility in a $0.10$ mol L$^{-1}$ solution of lead(II) nitrate, at $25^\circ$C.
questions.answer:
In $0.10$ M $\text{Pb(NO}_3)_2$, let the solubility be $x$: $K_{sp}=(x+0.10)(x)=7.40\times10^{-14}$. Since $x\ll0.10$: $0.10x=7.40\times10^{-14}\Rightarrow x=7.4\times10^{-13}$ mol L$^{-1}$.

In water the solubility is $2.72\times10^{-7}$ mol L$^{-1}$. Lead(II) carbonate is about $3.7\times10^{5}$ times less soluble in $0.10$ M lead(II) nitrate than in water, because of the common ion effect of $\text{Pb}^{2+}$.

questions.question: $25$ mL of $0.015$ M lead(II) nitrate solution and $50$ mL of $0.0030$ M sodium carbonate solution are mixed. Does precipitation of lead(II) carbonate occur? Support your answer with calculations.
questions.answer:
$n(\text{Pb}^{2+})=0.015\times0.025=3.75\times10^{-4}$ mol; $n(\text{CO}_3^{2-})=0.0030\times0.050=1.5\times10^{-4}$ mol. Total volume $=75$ mL, so
$[\text{Pb}^{2+}]=\dfrac{3.75\times10^{-4}}{0.075}=5.0\times10^{-3}$ M and $[\text{CO}_3^{2-}]=\dfrac{1.5\times10^{-4}}{0.075}=2.0\times10^{-3}$ M.
Ion product $Q=(5.0\times10^{-3})(2.0\times10^{-3})=1.0\times10^{-5}$.
Since $Q>K_{sp}$ ($7.40\times10^{-14}$), a precipitate of lead(II) carbonate forms.

questions.question: The solubility of ammonium chloride may be determined by back titration. A $20.0$ mL aliquot of the diluted saturated solution was added to $10.0$ mL of $0.400$ M NaOH. The solution was heated to drive off the ammonia formed, and the excess hydroxide ions were neutralised by $14.7$ mL of $0.125$ M HCl. Write an equation for the neutralisation reaction (in the titration).
questions.answer: $\text{NaOH}(aq)+\text{HCl}(aq)\rightarrow\text{NaCl}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$ (or $\text{OH}^-(aq)+\text{H}^+(aq)\rightarrow\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$).

questions.question: A $5.00$ mL saturated solution of ammonium chloride, $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ at $20.0^\circ$C was diluted to $250.0$ mL. A $20.0$ mL aliquot was added to $10.0$ mL of $0.400$ M NaOH (heated to drive off ammonia), and the excess hydroxide was neutralised by $14.7$ mL of $0.125$ M HCl. The molar mass of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ is $53.5\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. Calculate the solubility, in g L$^{-1}$, of ammonium chloride in water at $20^\circ$C.
questions.answer:
$n(\text{NaOH})_{added}=0.400\times0.0100=4.00\times10^{-3}$ mol
$n(\text{NaOH})_{excess}=n(\text{HCl})=0.125\times0.0147=1.8375\times10^{-3}$ mol
$n(\text{NaOH})$ reacted with $\text{NH}_4^+=4.00\times10^{-3}-1.84\times10^{-3}=2.1625\times10^{-3}$ mol $=n(\text{NH}_4\text{Cl})$ in the $20.0$ mL aliquot
In the $250.0$ mL (which came from the $5.00$ mL): $2.1625\times10^{-3}\times\dfrac{250.0}{20.0}=0.02703$ mol
In $1$ L of saturated solution: $0.02703\times\dfrac{1000}{5.00}=5.406$ mol
$$m=5.406\times53.5=289\ \text{g L}^{-1}$$

questions.question: If the burette was rinsed with water instead of acid before the titration, how would the calculated solubility of ammonium chloride be affected? Explain your answer.
questions.answer: The solubility would be **lower** than the true value. Water left in the burette dilutes the HCl, so a larger volume (titre) is needed to neutralise the excess NaOH. The calculated amount of excess NaOH is then too high, so the calculated amount of NaOH that reacted with $\text{NH}_4^+$ ($4.00\times10^{-3}-n_{excess}$) is too low. This gives too low a value for the moles of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ and hence for the solubility.

questions.question: A gravimetric analysis was undertaken to determine the percentage, by mass, of sulfur in a sample of lawn fertiliser. A $10.4$ g sample of fertiliser containing sulfate was dissolved into $250.0$ mL of distilled water, then divided into ten equal $25.0$ mL sub-samples. Various volumes of barium chloride solution were added to each sub-sample and the precipitate of barium sulfate was collected, dried and weighed. The graph shows the results (the mass of $\text{BaSO}_4$ levels off at $1.25$ g). Determine the percentage of sulfur, by mass, in the original sample of lawn fertiliser. Show all relevant working.
questions.answer:
The mass of fertiliser in each $25.0$ mL sub-sample is $\dfrac{10.4}{10}=1.04$ g. When excess $\text{BaCl}_2$ has been added the mass of $\text{BaSO}_4$ levels off at its maximum, $1.25$ g.
$M(\text{BaSO}_4)=137.3+32.07+4(16.00)=233.4$ g mol$^{-1}$
$n(\text{BaSO}_4)=\dfrac{1.25}{233.4}=5.36\times10^{-3}$ mol $=n(\text{S})$
$m(\text{S})=5.36\times10^{-3}\times32.07=0.172$ g
$$\%\text{S}=\frac{0.172}{1.04}\times100=16.5\%$$

questions.question: A student was given the organic compounds but-1-ene ($M=56$), 1-fluoropropane (62), propan-1-ol (60) and ethanamide (59). Predict and explain the different water solubilities of these compounds. Support your answer with at least ONE labelled diagram using structural formulas.
questions.answer:
The four compounds are neutral molecules of similar molar mass, so they have dispersion forces of similar size. Solubility depends on how strongly each can interact with water molecules (which form hydrogen bonds and dipole–dipole attractions) compared with the attractions between water molecules.

- **But-1-ene** is non-polar. It can only form weak dispersion forces with water and cannot form hydrogen bonds, so it is insoluble.
- **1-Fluoropropane** has a polar C–F bond, giving dipole–dipole attractions with water, and the F atom (with lone pairs) can accept a hydrogen bond from water, but the non-polar propyl chain is significant, so it is only slightly soluble.
- **Propan-1-ol** has a polar –OH group that can form hydrogen bonds with water (the O–H hydrogen bonds to the oxygen of water, and the oxygen accepts a hydrogen bond from water), so it is much more soluble (the short non-polar chain limits it only slightly).
- **Ethanamide** has a polar $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{–NH}_2$ group, which can form several hydrogen bonds with water (N–H···O and C=O···H–O), so it is very soluble.

Labelled diagram: a hydrogen bond between the hydroxyl group of propan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{–O}^{\delta-}\text{–H}^{\delta+}\cdots:\text{O}^{\delta-}\text{H}_2$ (dashed line = hydrogen bond between the $\text{H}^{\delta+}$ of one molecule and the lone pair on the oxygen of the other), and similarly for the $\text{N–H}$ and $\text{C=O}$ of ethanamide with water.

questions.question: Esterification is a reversible reaction that can undergo hydrolysis when heated with dilute sulfuric acid solution to drive the reaction towards the reactants. The flow chart shows reactions involving organic compounds A to F: the ester $\text{CH}_3\text{COOC(CH}_3)_3$ is heated with dilute sulfuric acid to give A and B; A reacts with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ to give C; B has no reaction with $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7/\text{H}^+$; B heated with concentrated sulfuric acid gives D; D reacted with hydrogen iodide gives E and F; F heated with warm KOH solution gives B. Draw the structure of each compound, A to F.
questions.answer:
- **A:** ethanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$
- **B:** 2-methylpropan-2-ol, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COH}$ (a tertiary alcohol, so it is not oxidised by acidified dichromate)
- **C:** sodium ethanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-\text{Na}^+$ (from the acid + sodium carbonate)
- **D:** 2-methylpropene, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C=CH}_2$ (dehydration of B)
- **E:** 1-iodo-2-methylpropane, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{I}$ (minor product of addition of HI)
- **F:** 2-iodo-2-methylpropane, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CI}$ (major product by Markovnikov's rule, which on heating with KOH is substituted back to B)

questions.question: The table shows acid dissociation constants at 25 °C: nitrous acid $\text{HNO}_2$ $7.2\times10^{-4}$; hydrofluoric acid HF $6.6\times10^{-4}$; hydrocyanic acid HCN $6.2\times10^{-10}$; propanoic acid $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ $1.34\times10^{-5}$; chlorous acid $\text{HClO}_2$ $1.1\times10^{-2}$. Identify the weakest acid in the table and determine the p$K_a$ value for this acid at 25 °C.
questions.answer: The weakest acid has the smallest $K_a$: hydrocyanic acid, HCN. $\text{p}K_a=-\log(6.2\times10^{-10})=9.21$.

questions.question: Identify the weakest base formed from these acids (those in the table of $K_a$ values above). What is the p$K_b$ for this base at 25 °C?
questions.answer: The strongest acid has the weakest conjugate base. The strongest acid is chlorous acid ($K_a=1.1\times10^{-2}$), so the weakest base is the chlorite ion, $\text{ClO}_2^-$. $\text{p}K_a=-\log(1.1\times10^{-2})=1.96$, so $\text{p}K_b=14.00-1.96=12.04$.

questions.question: Calculate the pH of a $0.010$ M solution of propanoic acid ($K_a=1.34\times10^{-5}$) at $25^\circ$C.
questions.answer:
$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COO}^-(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$. With $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]=[\text{A}^-]=x$ and $[\text{HA}]\approx0.010$ (as $x$ is small):
$$K_a=\frac{x^2}{0.010}=1.34\times10^{-5}\Rightarrow x=3.66\times10^{-4}\ \text{M},\quad\text{pH}=-\log(3.66\times10^{-4})=3.44$$

questions.question: A buffer solution is prepared by combining $100$ mL of $0.010$ M nitrous acid ($K_a=7.2\times10^{-4}$) and $80$ mL of $0.010$ M $\text{NaNO}_2$. Calculate the pH of this buffer solution and explain the classification of the solution as a buffer.
questions.answer:
After mixing (total volume $180$ mL): $[\text{HNO}_2]=\dfrac{0.010\times100}{180}=5.56\times10^{-3}$ M; $[\text{NO}_2^-]=\dfrac{0.010\times80}{180}=4.44\times10^{-3}$ M.
$$K_a=\frac{[\text{NO}_2^-][\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]}{[\text{HNO}_2]}\Rightarrow[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]=7.2\times10^{-4}\times\frac{5.56\times10^{-3}}{4.44\times10^{-3}}=9.0\times10^{-4}\ \text{M}$$
(the changes due to ionisation are negligible compared with the concentrations), so $\text{pH}=3.05$.

**Buffer:** the solution contains a weak acid ($\text{HNO}_2$) and its conjugate base ($\text{NO}_2^-$) in comparable concentrations. If a small amount of strong acid is added, $\text{NO}_2^-$ reacts with the added $\text{H}^+$; if a small amount of strong base is added, $\text{HNO}_2$ reacts with the added $\text{OH}^-$. By Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium $\text{HNO}_2+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightleftharpoons\text{NO}_2^-+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ shifts to counteract the change, so the pH remains almost constant at about 3.05.

questions.question: A series of chemical reactions can be used to distinguish between a variety of organic liquids. Draw a flowchart which could be used to distinguish between the following organic liquids: hex-1-ene, hexane, propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol. Include all reagents used and observations made.
questions.answer:
**Step 1: add bromine water to a sample of each liquid.**
- Hex-1-ene: the orange/brown bromine water is rapidly decolourised (addition reaction across the C=C bond).
- Hexane, propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol: no decolourisation.

**Step 2: add water to a sample of each of the remaining three liquids.**
- Hexane: immiscible, forming two layers (non-polar).
- Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol: miscible (dissolve in water to form a single layer).

**Step 3: to a sample of each alcohol add acidified potassium dichromate and heat under reflux (the solution turns from orange to green with both), then distil off the product and test it with sodium carbonate solution.**
- Propan-1-ol is oxidised to propanoic acid, which gives bubbles of carbon dioxide with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$.
- Propan-2-ol is oxidised to propanone (a ketone), which does not react with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ (no bubbles).

*(The school's flowchart used the Lucas test (anhydrous ZnCl$_2$/conc. HCl) to distinguish the alcohols; that test is not in the 2017 syllabus, so an oxidation-product test is used here.)*

questions.question: Write balanced equations for TWO reactions used in your flowchart using structural formulae.
questions.answer:
1. Addition of bromine to hex-1-ene: $\text{CH}_2\text{=CH–CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3+\text{Br}_2\rightarrow\text{CH}_2\text{Br–CHBr–CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$
2. Oxidation of propan-1-ol: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}+2[\text{O}]\rightarrow\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}+\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (using $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}/\text{H}^+$)
(or propan-2-ol: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3+[\text{O}]\rightarrow\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3+\text{H}_2\text{O}$.)

questions.question: Predict which of the 4 organic liquids (hex-1-ene, hexane, propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol) would have the highest boiling point. Explain your prediction.
questions.answer: **Propan-1-ol** would have the highest boiling point. Hex-1-ene and hexane are non-polar, so their only intermolecular forces are weak dispersion forces (they have similar molar masses). Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol have an –OH group and form hydrogen bonds as well as dispersion forces; hydrogen bonds are much stronger, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules. Propan-1-ol has a straight chain and a more exposed –OH group than propan-2-ol (whose –OH is on the middle carbon, which is more shielded and with a more branched shape), so it forms stronger intermolecular forces and has a higher boiling point than propan-2-ol.
